items.title: Soil erosion: US formula used worldwide produces unreliable figures in the Global South
items.summary: Rain and wind erode fertile soil worldwide. The topsoil, where plants take root and where most of the nutrients are found, is washed away from fields by heavy rain, particularly on slopes and where the ground is not covered by vegetation. Once washed away, it takes a very long time to reform—spanning decades to centuries. To estimate how much soil is lost, researchers use computational models.

items.summary: Alienware’s AW2726DM QD-OLED gaming monitor was a great deal even at its original $349.99 price. The low price and impressive specs were enough to convince me to get one at launch, and I’m glad that I did . I’m a little jealous that you have the opportunity to save $70 on the monitor I’ve been using for work and play for several months. Best Buy and Dell are selling the 27-inch 1440p monitor for $279.99 ahead of Black Friday. Alienware AW2726DM QD-OLED monitor If you’re on a tight budget, but want spectacular contrast and brightness control that only an OLED can provide, here’s a deal for you. Alienware’s 1440p 27-inch QD-OLED monitor with 240Hz refresh rate is selling at its lowest price yet. Read our hands-on . Where to Buy: $349.99 $279.99 at Best Buy $349.99 $279.99 at Dell The AW2726DM has more features than other similarly-priced monitors that I was comparing it to, and that still holds true when comparing it to more modern models. It has a 1440p QD-OLED screen that delivers tremendous contrast and deep blacks, and its 240Hz refresh rate provides a high ceiling for my graphics card to deliver fast frames. It’s equipped with HDMI and DisplayPort inputs, and really one of its only flaws is that it lacks USB-C video support. The monitor works great for PC games, as well as console titles. I think it’d be a sweet gift to yourself or to a gamer in your life this holiday. Read my Alienware AW2726DM hands-on.

This shift, called redshift, tells astronomers that we see the galaxy as it was when the universe was about 1.3 billion years old.

items.originalTitle: Thanksgiving Dinner Set to Cost Americans More This Year, Says Farm Bureau. Here’s Why
items.author: Callum Sutherland
items.title: Thanksgiving Dinner Set to Cost Americans More This Year, Says Farm Bureau. Here’s Why
items.summary: A group of friends celebrate the Thanksgiving Holiday with a "Friendsgiving" dinner. —Stock photo—Getty Images The American Farm Bureau Federation (AFBF) estimates that the cost of Thanksgiving dinner this year will be up more than 6% compared to last year, with steep turkey prices and higher fuel costs driving up the bill. The average 10-person dinner will cost $58.63, compared to $55.18 in 2025, according to the bureau’s annual report . This is the first year the bureau has reported a rise in the cost of the dinner since 2022, when prices hit a record high of $64.05. The agricultural organization’s estimates are based on hundreds of volunteer shoppers from all 50 states and Puerto Rico reporting prices for a standard list of items at their local grocery store. Thanksgiving dinners in the Northeast are set to be the most expensive, while dinners in the South will again be the least expensive in the country, according to the survey. “We see regional differences based on where shoppers choose to shop,” says Dr. Faith Parum, deputy chief economist at the AFBF. She tells TIME that the cost of transportation differs across the country, too, as “depending on supply chains, more fuel may be needed and that gets factored into food costs.” The analysis points toward turkey prices as the main driver for the higher Thanksgiving dinner cost. The bureau notes that the average price of a 16-pound frozen bird stands at $23.68, an increase of $2.38, or 10%, from 2025. Data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) says that the average market price of 8-16lb turkeys has increased from 135.8 cents/lb last year to 175.5 cents/lb in 2026, a rise of 29.2%. Parum says one of the main impacts on turkey prices for Americans this year is a higher global demand. “Lean protein has really boosted demand worldwide for things like chicken and turkey,” she explains. Total U.S. exports of turkey meat for 2026 are projected to reach 461 million pounds by the end of the year, compared to 420 million pounds last year, according to the USDA . Other holiday essentials including milk, rolls, and cranberries have also driven up the cost of Thanksgiving dinner. —Getty Images Energy costs have pushed up the price of turkey and other perishable items Since the start of President Donald Trump’s war with Iran in February, severe disruption to the Strait of Hormuz , a vital trade route through which around a fifth of global oil production flowed before the conflict, has upended fuel costs . Diesel hit a record average of $6.53 per gallon in the U.S. in September, according to the American Automobile Association. Diesel is essential to the process of food production (it's used in heavy machinery and vehicles) and is also pivotal to the transportation of goods. “Diesel prices are very integral in food pricing. If you remember food price inflation after Russia invaded Ukraine [in 2022], a lot of that was due to high energy prices, so we're seeing similar things now,” says Parum, pointing to the high Thanksgiving prices seen in 2022, also due in part to inflation felt after the COVID pandemic. Ricky Volpe, a professor in agribusiness at California Polytechnic State University, says that spikes in energy prices have hit poultry production particularly hard. “The poultry supply chain is highly elastic, where we see upstream cost impacts pass through quickly and pretty efficiently," he says, noting how energy is a major upstream cost. “Unfortunately for holiday shoppers, the recent surge in energy prices reflects that.” Volpe says that cattle, for example, are fed and grown over a longer period of time than turkeys, and are therefore less impacted by immediate energy price shocks. As a perishable commodity, turkey also requires extra refrigeration during processing and transport compared to long shelf-life goods, hence the higher impact of energy prices compared to non-perishables. Milk also saw some of the largest year-over-year percentage gains. “It’s a product that is obviously highly perishable, requires careful temperature control, has a relatively brief supply chain from the dairy to the retail sector, and is very energy intensive,” says Volpe. Experts also cite a labor shortage in the agricultural industry as being a contributing factor to higher Thanksgiving dinner costs. The employment of agricultural workers is set to decline by 2% by 2035, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . Furthermore, a survey conducted by Purdue University in May found that 44% of farm owners who hire labor said they had at least some or a lot of difficulty hiring this year. Increased prices for cranberries primarily stem from “high labor and diesel costs,” says Parum. “We're really seeing a labor shortage in the United States for agricultural workers.” Turkey flocks continue to recover numbers after bird influenza spikes Turkey prices are also high due to a series of spikes in highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) cases in recent years. Rises in the number of cases in 2022 , 2023 and 2024 hit egg-laying hens and turkey, in particular . “We have seen a decrease in the number of cases, but it still takes time for those flocks to fully recover,” says Parum. The cost of turkey feed has also been on the rise this year, which has pushed up the price for consumers. Turkey feed in the U.S. is usually made up of corn and soybeans, both of which have become more costly to produce for farmers this year compared to last. According to the USDA, total operating costs for a planted acre of corn in 2025 was $455.80, compared to $496.92 in its 2026 forecast. For soybeans, this cost stood at $250.88, compared to a 2026 projection of $266.45. “The cost of planting was really high in the last season,” says Jada Thompson, an associate professor in agricultural economics and agribusiness at the University of Arkansas. “The cost of urea and fertilizer was so high that it was affecting farmers’ break-even price,” she adds, pointing to this factor as one reason for increased planting costs. Fertilizers such as urea saw a sharp rise in cost in the months following the start of the Iran war, hitting farmers particularly hard during the spring planting season . Turkeys for sale in a supermarket in Lafayette, California, on Nov. 13, 2025. —Smith Collection—Getty Images How can Americans save money on their Thanksgiving dinners? The cost-of-living crisis continues to be a key concern for Americans. After the Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections, an NBC exit poll found that 89% of Americans said the cost of living was a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress. Despite the higher cost of dinner as a whole, some items on the Thanksgiving table—such as frozen pie crust—are in fact cheaper than last year, according to the bureau. Experts say there are other ways that families can still cut back ahead of the holiday. Grocery stores often have sales for items such as turkey in the immediate build up to Thanksgiving. “A lot of retailers are looking to try to capture the [Thanksgiving] market,” says Thompson. “Oftentimes, what you'll see is a really high, heavy discount on turkeys.” Volpe notes that purchasing store-branded items, frozen turkeys instead of fresh, or waiting until closer to Thanksgiving to shop can also help bring the cost of dinner down. “If you're on a budget, if you're worried about affordability, these types of substitutions still mean real savings,” he says.

items.originalTitle: ‘Great Patriot and National Treasure’: Trump Applauds NVIDIA’s Decision to Reinstate Jensen Huang
items.author: Chantelle Lee
items.title: ‘Great Patriot and National Treasure’: Trump Applauds NVIDIA’s Decision to Reinstate Jensen Huang
items.summary: President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Marylandon Nov. 16, 2026. —Win McNamee—Getty Images President Donald Trump on Monday applauded NVIDIA’s board of directors for reinstating Jensen Huang as the company’s president and CEO, calling it “the correct and proper decision.” “The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO,” Trump said in a Truth Social post . “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” Huang’s return to the technology company comes 11 days after he resigned in scandal, amid news reports that he had an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. officials believed was a Chinese spy. The President said in his post on Monday, though, that the U.S. government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security” and that the U.S. Attorney General “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Trump went on to say that he considers Huang to be “a Great Patriot and National Treasure.” NVIDIA announced the news of Huang’s return on Monday morning, saying in a statement that the board “voted unanimously” on the move after having several conversations with Huang that left the board “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” The company added that the board “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” The company said that Huang’s reinstatement as president and CEO is effective immediately. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey C. Jones, chair of NVIDIA’s board of directors, said in a statement. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company.” Huang said that he was “honored” to resume leading the company. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” he said in a statement. “I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.” The night before, the President had expressed his desire for NVIDIA to reinstate Huang. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday evening. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.”

items.author: Ben Tracy of Climate Central
items.title: Cranberry jam: warming winters and extreme weather threaten an iconic holiday fruit
items.summary: Scientists are racing to identify and breed new berry varieties that can thrive on an increasingly warmer planet It is harvest time in rural Wisconsin , and the Badger state’s most vibrant crop is painting the rolling countryside a brilliant, unmistakable red. For nearly three decades, Nicole Hansen has been farming cranberries here. Wisconsin produces more than 60% of the nation’s supply. On a crisp fall morning, we waded into a marsh with her to round up the floating harvest. Climate Central is an independent group of scientists and communicators that researches and reports the facts about our changing climate and how it affects people’s lives
